
### one connection, multiple requests  {.smaller}


* HTTP/0.9, HTTP/1.0 --- one request+response per connection 

   * big efficiency problem

* solution 1: persistent connections
* solution 2: pipelining
* solution 3 (HTTP/2+): multiple ‘streams’ in one connection


### end-of-request/response  {.smaller}


* body of request/response can be variable length 
<hr class="vspace" />
* so when does request/response end if it has a body?
* HTTP/1.0 original solution (RFC 1945) 

   * ‘‘the length of that body may be determined in two ways. If a Content-Length field is present, the value in bytes represents the length of the Entity-Body. Otherwise, the body length is determined by the closing of the connection by the server.’’

* advantage of latter idea: don't need to generate whole document before sending headers
* disadvantage: no persistent connections!


### chunked transfer coding 


<pre><code>HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Content-Type: text/plain
<em>Transfer-Coding: chunked</em>
...

<span style="border: 2px solid red">1B</span>
<em>This is 0x1B bytes of text.</em>
<span style="border: 2px solid red">21</span>
<em>And 0x21 bytes</em>
<em>with more lines.</em>
<span style="border: 2px solid red">0</span>
</code></pre>


### pipelining 

![](/http/texfig/persistent-pipelining.figure.svg){fig-alt="client->server: GET /image1, GET /image2, GET /script (before getting replies). server-> client: HTTP/1.1 200 OK ..., HTTP/1.1 200 OK ..., HTTP/1.1 200 OK ..."}


### HTTP/1.1 ‘pipelining’ 


* send series of requests before receiving any response
* potentailly server can potentially process requests in parallel 
<hr class="vspace" />
* need to handle resending requests if connection dropped early


### HTTP/2.0 multiple streams 


![](/http/http2-multi-reqres){fig-alt="wireshark screenshot of HTTP/2 session, where the client sends many sets of headers: GET /wiki/, GET /w/load.php?..., GET /static/images/icons/..., ... Each set of headers is sent in a separate stream ID identified like by text like [15] in 'HEADERS[15]: GET /wiki/...' in the wireshark display. The server sends response chunks marked similary HEADERS[15]: 301 Moved Permanatelty; HEADERS[17]: 200 OK; DATA[17], ... In this session the responses are mostly sent in the order they are requested."}
